sections.html:
Two Hernando offices split the work. The Tax Assessor decides what a parcel is worth, and the Tax Collector sends the bill and takes the money. Collector: 365 Losher Street, Suite 110, Hernando, 662-469-8030, plus a branch on BJ Chain Drive in Olive Branch. Assessor: 365 Losher Street, Suite 100, 662-469-8029.

Real property gets a fresh valuation at least every four years under Mississippi law, and taxable personal property every year. Nobody has to walk through your house to do it. You never vote on your own rate. Instead the county, the city and the school district each state a budget need, and local officials convert those into one millage figure.

Mississippi property classes and assessment ratios
ClassWhat it coversAssessment ratio
Class ISingle-family, owner-occupied home10%
Class IIOther real property, such as rentals and land15%
Class IIIBusiness personal property15%
Class IVPublic utility property30%
Class VMotor vehicles30%

Your bill is true value, times the ratio for your class, times millage. A rental house sits in Class II, so more of its value is taxed than on an owner-occupied home.

Ownership on January 1 fixes who is assessed. Bills arrive in November and December, and February 1 is the due date. When that day lands on a weekend or holiday, the next Monday works with no penalty or interest.

Taxes left unpaid on real estate can send the parcel to the county tax sale. Counties differ: some hold it the first Monday in April, others the last Monday in August. Ask the collector for your date.

  • Whoever buys at the sale does not get clean title at once, because the owner has two years from the sale to redeem under Miss. Code Ann. 27-45-3.
  • A parcel that draws no bidder passes to the State of Mississippi, where the Secretary of State manages it at 1-866-835-2637.
  • Back taxes cloud the title, so the title company will insist on payment at closing.

Appeals start with a hearing request to the county Board of Supervisors, handled through the Chancery Clerk. File by the first Monday in August, ahead of the tax due date.

Call the assessor first and bring comparable sales or repair bids. Photos and contractor quotes for a bad roof or a cracked foundation beat opinion. Because the board reviews values, hears objections and adopts the rolls in the summer, the August date is firm.

A homestead exemption reduces the bill, but it does not follow the house to a new owner. File with the Tax Assessor between January 1 and April 1. After that you need not refile each year unless ownership or marital status changes.

Owners aged 65 or older, and totally disabled owners who otherwise qualify, owe no tax on the first $75,000 of true value. The exemption is denied when the owner or spouse is behind on state income tax or has a vehicle tagged outside the home county. If you are buying, file in your first year, since a missed April 1 pushes the benefit to the next assessment year.

Many sellers close with a balance due. Your title company requests a payoff number and subtracts it from your proceeds at the table. If the parcel was already sold at a tax sale, that redemption amount is also owed, and the two-year redemption window applies.

Local sellers tend to run into the same few problems:

  • Check that the owner name, mailing address and homestead status on the roll are current, since a bill sent to the wrong address is still due.
  • Inherited homes can carry unpaid taxes or unrecorded paperwork that must be cleared before closing.
  • Rentals in Class II carry a higher assessment ratio, which matters when you sell a tenant-occupied house.
  • Newer subdivisions can sit in a city levy, while a house outside city limits does not, so two similar homes can have different bills.

A cash sale can shorten that list because the buyer purchases as-is and closes on a date you choose. You still need a clean title, a payoff for any mortgage and the current tax paid or settled on the closing statement.

sections.h2: Checking what you owe before you sell
sections.html:
Start with the county's online tax search, which lists real and personal property by name, parcel or address and shows amounts due. Then confirm with the collector by phone, since tax-sale and prior-year balances can appear separately.

  1. Find the parcel number on your deed or the assessor's lookup.
  2. Check the current and prior-year balances with the Tax Collector in Hernando or Olive Branch.
  3. Ask the Chancery Clerk whether any past sale exists on the parcel.
  4. Give your title company the figures so they can settle taxes at closing.

This page is general information, not legal or tax advice. Confirm every date and amount with the county office before you rely on it.

sections.h2: How DeSoto County is laid out
sections.html:
DeSoto County sits in the northwest corner of Mississippi, directly south of Shelby County, Tennessee, and the county seat is Hernando. Most people live in four cities: Hernando, Horn Lake, Olive Branch and Southaven. The county also has the town of Walls, census-designated places such as Lake View, Lynchburg and Pleasant Hill, and unincorporated communities like Lake Cormorant, Nesbit and Cockrum.

Where a house sits decides which city or school levy shows up on the bill, so a seller's first step is to look at the parcel's tax district. The census counted 185,314 people in 2020, and the 2025 estimate is 197,918. One school district, the DeSoto County School District, serves the whole county, though attendance zones still differ by address.

The county farmed cotton first, then dairy and soybeans, before subdivisions replaced the fields. Homes in Southaven went on sale in 1958, and Interstate 55 opened through Hernando in 1964. The population was 67,910 in 1990 and reached 161,252 by 2010. Houses here span several building eras: a 1970s ranch in Horn Lake and a 2010s two-story in Olive Branch face different repair lists, even though the same collector bills both.

Interstate 55, Interstate 69, Interstate 269, U.S. 51 and U.S. 61 carry most traffic. The county has no fixed-route transit of its own, so most households depend on a car.

faqs.q: When are DeSoto County property taxes due?
faqs.a: By February 1 for property assessed the year before. A weekend or holiday on that date moves the penalty-free deadline to the next Monday.

faqs.q: Where do I pay property tax in DeSoto County?
faqs.a: The DeSoto County Tax Collector takes payment in Hernando at 365 Losher Street, Suite 110 (662-469-8030) and at the Olive Branch branch. Call ahead about hours and payment types.

faqs.q: How do I appeal my DeSoto County assessment?
faqs.a: Ask the Chancery Clerk to put you before the Board of Supervisors. File by the first Monday in August, before the tax comes due.

faqs.q: Can I sell a DeSoto County house with taxes owed?
faqs.a: Yes. Yes. The title company asks for a payoff figure and pays the taxes from your proceeds at closing. A parcel already sold at a tax sale also needs its redemption amount settled.

faqs.q: Does DeSoto County have one school district?
faqs.a: Yes. The DeSoto County School District serves the whole county and is the largest in Mississippi. Confirm attendance zones with the district for a specific address.
